articles.title: Visa delays and policy uncertainty projected to reduce foreign enrolment in the US by more than 100,000 students this fall
articles.summary: A new analysis by NAFSA and JB International projects that visa processing delays and upcoming policy changes will reduce international student enrolment in the United States by more than 100,000 students this fall. The projection is based on institutional responses collected in IIE’s Spring 2026 Snapshot on International Educational Exchange.
articles.insight:
This news signals potential softening in US demand for international students, driven by documented visa delays and policy uncertainty—though it remains unclear whether this reflects broader global sentiment shifts or is largely US-specific due to its unique immigration challenges.  
Admissions teams should monitor real-time application trends from key source markets, track competitor institutions’ enrolment data, and assess whether prospective students are expressing heightened concerns about visa timelines or post-study work prospects in their outreach and counselling interactions.

articles.title: Report: US considering a $100,000 fee for Optional Practical Training
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration is considering imposing a $100,000 fee on international students seeking Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorization to work in the U.S. after graduating from an American university. This potential policy change was disclosed by people familiar with the matter and was first published by ICEF Monitor.
articles.insight:
This proposed $100,000 OPT fee—though unconfirmed and potentially subject to legal or political reversal—could dampen U.S. appeal for international students weighing post-study work value, especially among cost-sensitive markets in Asia and Latin America, thereby indirectly intensifying competition for talent elsewhere.  
Admissions teams should track official USCIS/ICE guidance and consult legal partners on OPT policy trajectories, while benchmarking how peer institutions in the UK, Australia, and New Zealand are positioning their post-study work offerings relative to evolving U.S. uncertainty.

articles.title: RMIT Vietnam secures approval for new Hanoi campus and Saigon South expansion
articles.summary: RMIT University has received approval from the Vietnamese government to establish a new campus in Hanoi. It has also secured approval to redevelop its existing Saigon South campus in Ho Chi Minh City.
articles.insight:
RMIT Vietnam’s campus expansion signals growing institutional confidence in Vietnam’s higher education market, potentially reflecting stronger domestic demand and indirect pressure on regional recruitment as Southeast Asian students weigh increasingly competitive local options alongside traditional Anglophone destinations.  

Admissions teams should monitor Vietnamese student enrolment trends across their institutions, track RMIT Vietnam’s programme offerings and fee structures, and assess whether this development correlates with shifts in outbound mobility patterns or scholarship uptake from key Southeast Asian source regions.

articles.title: U.K. government pauses Chevening Fellowships for a year over likely budget cuts
articles.summary: The U.K. government has paused Chevening Fellowships for one year due to anticipated budget cuts. This pause affects the CRISP programme for science and innovation, the cybersecurity fellowship, and the South Asia Journalism Programme, while Chevening Scholarships remain open.
articles.insight:
The pause in Chevening Fellowships—particularly the South Asia Journalism Programme—may modestly reduce short-term demand for UK-based professional development opportunities, though broader undergraduate and postgraduate student flows remain unaffected and Chevening Scholarships continue as usual.  
Admissions teams should monitor whether partner institutions in South Asia report shifts in applicant interest toward alternative destinations or programmes, and assess if their outreach can strategically highlight complementary funded opportunities amid evolving UK government priorities.

articles.title: Nearly 31% fewer Indians are moving abroad to study: What is making students lose appetite for overseas education?
articles.summary: Overseas student departures from India have declined for two consecutive years after peaking in 2023, with nearly 31% fewer Indian students moving abroad to study. This drop is attributed to rising education costs, tighter visa regulations, uncertain job prospects, and evolving immigration policies.
articles.insight:
This decline signals potential softening in Indian student demand for overseas study, likely driven by cost and immigration concerns—but it remains unclear whether this reflects a structural shift or temporary headwinds amid broader global mobility trends.  
Admissions teams should track quarterly visa issuance data, scholarship uptake rates, and competitor pricing strategies in India, while reviewing value propositions around post-study work pathways and affordability to gauge resilience in this key source market.

articles.title: Thailand steps up crackdown on foreigners engaged in illegal business activities
articles.summary: Thailand has intensified enforcement actions against illegal business networks and suspected nominee shareholding by conducting joint inspections of hotels and other establishments in Bangkok’s Huai Khwang District. The Government Public Relations Department reported this crackdown.
articles.insight:
This news may indirectly affect student demand from Southeast Asia if perceptions of Thailand as a regional study or work destination shift due to stricter enforcement of business regulations, though no direct link to student visas or education policy is evident.  
Admissions teams should monitor Thai government communications on visa categories and consult local agents about any emerging concerns among prospective students regarding post-study work options or third-country residency plans.
